title: SRE request audit and error postmortem walkthrough - GlacioTech

Priya to spin up a scoped benchmark in Redwood sandbox and share results by 2025-08-20
GlacioTech to provide postmortem doc and sample logs by 2025-08-18

summary: GlacioTech SREs walked through a recent production incident and wanted a live Console walkthrough: request correlation, trace export, error classification, and how Redwood supports audit logs and private deployments. AE+SE demoed the request inspector, trace timeline, and how to attach postmortem artifacts to requests. Action items: share traces, run a scoped Redwood benchmark, and exchange security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (GlacioTech SRE Lead), Tom Reyes (GlacioTech Eng Manager), Ben Ortiz (GlacioTech Platform Eng)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh we got about 50 minutes, I'm Jordan, AE on the account, with Priya who is our SE.
[00:07] Priya Raman: hi all, thanks for carving out time. I saw the postmortem you sent, Aisha, super helpful. we'll try to map to the console flows you asked about.
[00:15] Aisha Khan: yeah hi, thanks. the big thing for us is reproducibility of the error, and being able to pull full request context for audits, like we had a compliance ask last week.
[00:26] Tom Reyes: and latency tail was pretty bad — right? some requests spiked to 3.5s whereas our SLO is 250ms for interactive features.
[00:34] Ben Ortiz: also want to understand how kv cache + batching affects root cause, because we saw token duplication in one run.
[00:41] Jordan Lee: absolutely, that's exactly what Priya and I planned to show: request inspector, trace timeline, correlation IDs, and how to export traces and logs for your storage, plus our audit log pipeline.

[02:05] Priya Raman: loading my screen now, I'm in the Redwood Console — though sometimes my browser shows it as "Redwood Consoled" in captions, ignore that —
[02:14] Aisha Khan: haha saw that in the deck, wondered if i had a weird browser plugin.
[02:19] Priya Raman: okay so first thing, top-left you can search by request id, or by user id, or by a custom correlation tag. i'll run a sample query for the request ids you sent in the postmortem, the UI will show timeline, status codes, token counts, and any retry/fallback events.
[02:40] Priya Raman: (typing) for this request: request-id glc-57f2b1 — you can see the trace pane, it shows our kernel selection step, kv cache hit/miss events, batching window, and the latency per hop.
[02:58] Ben Ortiz: can you zoom one level into the kv cache event? it looked like there was a partial hit which then forced a rerun of decode.
[03:07] Priya Raman: yeah see here — the cache key mismatched due to a whitespace normalization issue — often transcription or prompt templating causes that. the trace marks it as cache_miss -> partial_prefetch -> full_load, which added ~480ms.
[03:30] Tom Reyes: interesting, we do have a preprocessor that normalizes whitespace but maybe not for these legacy endpoints.

[04:05] Aisha Khan: quick question: how long do these request traces live in Console? retention and audit concerns are big for us.
[04:12] Jordan Lee: default is 30 days in the hosted product, but for Dedicated and Private you control retention — we can forward all traces to your S3/Cloud Storage or to your SIEM for long term retention.
[04:26] Aisha Khan: okay perfect — and are those exports hashed/encrypted with our KMS?
[04:31] Priya Raman: yes, when you configure a dedicated pipeline we support customer-managed keys; exports can be encrypted and the export logs include a manifest for rehydration.

[05:15] Priya Raman: back to the trace: if you expand the decode operation you'll see function calls for tokenization, kernel dispatch, and our fallback path when a quantized kernel doesn't support a certain op. that fallback is where we sometimes see a 200-300ms penalty if fallback to a reference kernel is triggered.
[05:40] Ben Ortiz: is that fallback deterministic? can we pin model variants to avoid it?
[05:45] Priya Raman: yes you can pin a model variant or a quantization profile per route; also our Optimize suggestions can recommend a quant profile that's compatible. we'll show the policy later.

[06:20] Jordan Lee: want to pause and confirm the key observations from your postmortem — Aisha, do you want to summarize the incident quickly so we make sure the demo lines up?
[06:30] Aisha Khan: sure. we had a burst around 02:00 UTC on 8/9 where a small percentage of requests experienced high latency and token duplication in outputs. root cause we identified as a combination of mixed embedding batch size and a misnormalized prompt that caused cache misses. testers re-ran and sometimes couldn't reproduce.
[06:51] Priya Raman: that matches what I see in the exported traces you attached. i'm going to show you how we'd recreate and then how we'd instrument the flow to make future incidents resolvable in less than an hour.

[08:00] Priya Raman: step one is searching by time window and trace tag. Priya: searching by event.group = "glac-incident-0809" — results come back, click open and you get the waterfall. see the repeated generate calls? those are retries from the routing layer when an intermediate timeout happened.
[08:22] Tom Reyes: those retries — are they automatic? is that from our retry policy?
[08:26] Jordan Lee: the runtime has a smart retry layer that retries idempotent requests depending on route policy; you can tune it per route or disable it. retries are a common cause of amplification if upstream timeouts are too aggressive.

[09:12] Priya Raman: i also want to show the error classification tags. Console auto-classifies errors into transient, resource, and model-failure buckets based on heuristics — transcriptions sometimes call it "model fault" — and you can override these or add custom tags.
[09:30] Aisha Khan: can those classifications be surfaced to our PagerDuty alerts?
[09:34] Priya Raman: yes we push alerts via webhook and you can map tags to severity -> PagerDuty, Slack, or email.

[10:05] Ben Ortiz: we're also worried about the black box: when a fallback happens we only see a high-level note, not the exact kernel selection. can you show what the export includes?
[10:15] Priya Raman: absolutely — if you click export trace you get a JSON with the entire timeline, kernel ids, latency, mem usage, and any fallback stack traces; note: for hosted customers some low-level traces are redacted for security but for Dedicated/Private we can include full kernel traces under an NDA.
[10:38] Aisha Khan: that's good to know. we'll need that for audits.

[12:00] Jordan Lee: quick aside — curious if you considered Dedicated or Private for this workload? Sounds like audit and long retention are drivers.
[12:08] Aisha Khan: yeah our security team pushed for a private option because of logs and KMS. we also want more deterministic performance for the SLOs.
[12:16] Tom Reyes: budget-wise we'll likely start with Dedicated and see if Private is needed.

[12:45] Priya Raman: ok next, i'll recreate the failing flow live with a small sandbox. i've uploaded a synthetic batch that mirrors your production distribution — note: i'm using Redwood sandbox region which may have slightly different kernel versions so numbers are illustrative.
[13:05] Priya Raman: running the batch now... you can see streaming on the right, the trace began, and a few requests have a cache_miss event followed by prefetch and decode. total extra time here ~520ms on two requests.
[13:28] Ben Ortiz: can we toggle prefetch behavior? our prefetch window might be too short.
[13:32] Priya Raman: yes, prefetch is tunable per route: window size, max prefetch tokens, and you can disable aggressive prefetch. optimize also suggests settings.

[14:10] Priya Raman: i'm going to show how to attach a postmortem artifact to a request. click the request -> attachments -> upload postmortem. once attached the request view keeps a link to the doc and you can open it inline. this is handy for future incident reviews.
[14:31] Aisha Khan: nice — we want that so our SREs can jump from alert to full context quickly.

[15:50] Priya Raman: quick demo of the Request Inspector's filter language: you can do status==200 AND token_count>512 AND tags CONTAINS "glac-incident" — this becomes a saved view and you can schedule exports.
[16:12] Tom Reyes: saved views sound useful. can saved views run periodic exports to our S3?
[16:16] Jordan Lee: yep, you can wire a saved view to an export sink; schedule daily or on-demand.

[17:05] Aisha Khan: about the duplicated tokens in outputs — is that likely caused by the preprocessor mismatching or by batching reordering?
[17:12] Priya Raman: both are possible. in your traces we saw a preprocessor whitespace diff then a late batch reorder for two flows — the batch reorder led to a token stream being submitted twice to the decode kernel because a retry arrived late.
[17:30] Ben Ortiz: so we'd want stronger idempotency keys and tweak retry window?
[17:33] Priya Raman: exactly — add an idempotency header per user request and tighten retry policy for that route.

[18:00] Aisha Khan: security question: when traces are exported to our S3 do you leave any PII in the text?
[18:07] Jordan Lee: by default we redact user content fields for hosted exports, but for Dedicated/Private you control the redaction rules. we can support custom redaction pipelines before exporting.

[19:10] Priya Raman: i'm going to walk through an example export now — exporting this trace bundle -> progress bar -> done. downloading the JSON shows events, timings, kernel ids. you'll also get an md5 manifest and a signed URL for retrieval.
[19:35] Tom Reyes: does the signed URL expire?
[19:38] Priya Raman: yes, you configure expiry; defaults are 24 hours.

[20:20] Ben Ortiz: can we incrementally stream traces to our SIEM in near-real-time? we don't want batch exports for long windows.
[20:26] Jordan Lee: we have a real-time forwarder that streams events via Kafka or HTTPS to your SIEM; throughput is tunable.

[21:00] Aisha Khan: one more compliance question: audit logs for admin actions — who changed route config and when — is that part of the trace?
[21:08] Priya Raman: audit logs are a separate collection but linked by request tag; admin actions show up in the audit index and you can query by actor, action, and timestamp. those logs can also be exported to your retention store.

[22:30] Priya Raman: switching to the Console's Error Analysis tab: it surfaces top error classes, trend lines, and suggests root cause candidates — you can also upload your own detection rules. notice here it suggested two candidates: prefetch policy and retry amplification.
[22:55] Aisha Khan: can we annotate an error bucket with our internal postmortem?
[22:59] Priya Raman: yes you can attach notes to error buckets, link to tickets, and assign owners.

[24:05] Jordan Lee: quick clarifying Q — you mentioned token duplication in outputs only for some customers. is that reproducible via a specific feature flag?
[24:12] Tom Reyes: we have a legacy flag enabled on certain user cohorts, yes.

[25:00] Priya Raman: i'll also show how tracing ties into our rollout system: if you run a canary a/b you get per-variant traces and a side-by-side comparison in the Console, so you can see if variant B triggered more fallback paths.
[25:22] Ben Ortiz: that's helpful. we can correlate to cohort config.

[26:30] Priya Raman: now quick note on cost analysis tied to traces — Console surfaces token-level cost and you can attribute cost per route and per request. that helped customers find expensive micro-paths.
[26:52] Aisha Khan: our finance team will like that. any way to hide cost in the exported trace?
[26:57] Jordan Lee: cost fields can be redacted on export if you need.

[28:15] Priya Raman: ok i'm going to simulate a constrained capacity scenario — we throttle a pool and then watch the request timeline show queued events, evictions, and fallback to a smaller model. you can see the policy triggered and the request got a 202 fallback then retried.
[28:40] Tom Reyes: so fallback to smaller models is automatic? or only if policy allows?
[28:45] Priya Raman: it's policy-driven — you configure fallback tiers and priority. many customers prefer explicit canary fallbacks rather than automatic.

[30:05] Aisha Khan: if we go Dedicated what parts of the audit chain do we still depend on Redwood for?
[30:12] Jordan Lee: Redwood continues to provide the control plane and the Console UX; Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and options to own the export pipeline and KMS. Private moves the control plane into your VPC if you need full isolation.

[31:00] Ben Ortiz: any gotchas with Private on prem? like kernel parity or trace format differences?
[31:08] Priya Raman: kernel parity is a thing — on prem you can pick runtime versions but we recommend a compatibility window. trace format remains the same, but low-level fields may differ if you use different hardware.

[32:10] Tom Reyes: can we backfill traces into Console if we already have logs in our SIEM?
[32:16] Priya Raman: yes you can push historical events and link them by request id; Console will ingest and index them for search.

[33:25] Jordan Lee: quick check — is there anything you want us to run live for the five sample request ids you mentioned?
[33:32] Aisha Khan: yes if you can pull those and show the kernel fallback stacks and the full request body that'd be great.

[34:10] Priya Raman: pulling request glc-57f2b1 now... opening trace -> expanding fallback stack -> here we see the exact op that triggered fallback: einsum-like op not supported in quantized kernel, fallback to float kernel.
[34:36] Ben Ortiz: confirms the theory — we have a custom layer that does einsum for attention recompute.

[35:00] Priya Raman: i'll attach this trace export to the ticket and also include the kernel stack and suggested route tweaks.

[36:20] Aisha Khan: about instrumentation — what is the overhead of tracing? do we add measurable latency?
[36:26] Priya Raman: tracing is sampling-based by default; for full traces there's some overhead (single-digit ms) and for high QPS flows we recommend sampling plus targeted full traces for incidents.

[37:10] Tom Reyes: how do we correlate from our app logs to Redwood traces? do you accept a custom correlation header?
[37:16] Jordan Lee: yes we support a X-Glacio-Request-ID header or any custom header; Console will pick that up and index it. if absent we fall back to generated request ids.

[38:05] Ben Ortiz: what about retention costs? any guidance on sizing for 90-day retention in Dedicated?
[38:10] Priya Raman: we can run a cost projection; rough rule: trace size scales with token volume and event richness — we'll need a sample day of logs to estimate. that's something we'll include in the scoped benchmark.

[39:30] Jordan Lee: practical next step: Priya will export the traces for those five IDs and spin up a small benchmark with your production-ish distribution; i'll send the SOC2 + audit log docs.

[40:05] Aisha Khan: great, and we'll share the full postmortem with sample payloads and our redaction rules.

[41:00] Priya Raman: any remaining questions about debug workflows?
[41:07] Tom Reyes: curious about alert fatigue — can we route only severe error buckets through PD and have low severity in Slack?
[41:12] Priya Raman: yes, you can map error bucket -> severity -> sink. the Console's suggestion engine can also propose thresholds.

[42:20] Ben Ortiz: developer ergonomics — is there an API for the Request Inspector so our tools can fetch traces programmatically?
[42:26] Priya Raman: we have a REST API and SDKs; you can query traces, create saved views, and trigger exports. I'll share the API reference link.

[43:10] Jordan Lee: I'm going to summarize: 1) Priya will export the five traces and run a Redwood sandbox benchmark; 2) Jordan will send SOC2/security artifact and audit log options; 3) GlacioTech will share postmortem, sample payloads, and redaction rules; 4) schedule follow-up to review benchmark results.

[43:45] Aisha Khan: that matches. do we want a follow-up next week?
[43:49] Jordan Lee: yes let's aim for 2025-08-21, same time, pending benchmark readiness.

[44:10] Tom Reyes: one more nit: some field names in the trace JSON look different from our internal format, is there a mapping doc?
[44:18] Priya Raman: yes i'll attach a trace schema mapping and a sample transformation script.

[45:00] Ben Ortiz: any known limitations with large batch trace exports? we've seen exports fail for >10M events in other systems.
[45:08] Priya Raman: for very large exports we recommend chunked exports or streaming to your Kafka; full-bundle dumps are fine under a few million events, beyond that we suggest a streaming approach. We'll include recommended configs in the benchmark result.

[46:30] Aisha Khan: ok thanks all, feel pretty comfortable with the debugging flow now.

[47:05] Priya Raman: i'll also note the quick policy changes that would have prevented the incident: enforce idempotency header, tighten retry window, and increase prefetch window to reduce cache misses.

[48:00] Jordan Lee: great. i'll follow up with the SOC2 doc and schedule invite for next week. thanks for a thorough session.

[49:10] Tom Reyes: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[49:15] Ben Ortiz: thanks.
[49:20] Aisha Khan: thanks, bye.

[54:00] Meeting end.

Artifacts mentioned (in transcript text): GlacioTech postmortem link, trace export sample link, SOC2 + audit logging overview link, sandbox benchmark placeholder link.
